analysis.one_liner: Restores federal preclearance of voting rule changes and adds polling access guarantees on tribal lands.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 45 cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing or vote; it died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rebuild the Voting Rights Act's coverage formula, struck down by the Supreme Court in 2013, by putting states and localities with recent records of voting rights violations back under federal preclearance — meaning certain voting changes could not take effect until approved by the Justice Department or a federal court. It would also require states to provide polling places on tribal lands, force public notice of voting changes, and make it easier for voters to get a fast court order blocking a possibly discriminatory voting rule while an election nears. It never got past the committee referral stage.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters in jurisdictions with recent histories of voting rights violations — particularly Black, Hispanic, Asian American, and Native American voters — who would gain advance review of changes like new ID requirements, polling place closures, and redistricting plans. Tribal members on reservations would gain guaranteed nearby polling places, early voting locations, and registration offices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters of color and tribal members

how_it_helps.text: States with 15 or more voting rights violations in the previous 25 years, or 10 or more including one by the state itself, would again need federal approval before implementing new voting qualifications, standards, or procedures; individual subdivisions with 3 or more violations would be covered separately.

Tribes could require states to provide polling places, absentee and early voting locations, and voter registration offices on tribal lands at no cost to the tribe, with equal poll workers, hours, and equipment.

States and large localities would have to post public notice within 48 hours of changes to voting rules, and disclose polling place resources and the demographic effects of district changes before federal elections.
Courts would have to grant quick preliminary relief when a voter raises a serious question that a voting practice is discriminatory and the hardship on the voter outweighs the harm to the government.

The Justice Department could assign federal election observers to enforce bilingual voting requirements and to respond to tribal complaints, and jurisdictions could still qualify for exemptions by winning a declaratory judgment that they no longer discriminate.

analysis.who_pays: State and local election officials would bear the cost of submitting covered voting changes for federal review, posting detailed public notices, and providing additional polling resources on tribal lands. Jurisdictions with recent violations would lose the ability to change voting rules without federal approval during the 10-year coverage period.

drawbacks.text: The bill subjects even jurisdictions not historically covered to federal approval for specified voting changes, and a state's 25-year violation history could pull in many localities; election officials would face a 60-day federal review process before implementing changes to ID rules, polling locations, district boundaries, and more.

States would carry new administrative costs and paperwork — annual identification of covered practices, 48-hour public notice of voting changes, and disclosure of precinct-level demographics and machine assignments — which small jurisdictions in particular would have to absorb.

Coverage would rest on any final court judgment, settlement, or an Attorney General objection over a 25-year lookback, so a jurisdiction could be covered for practices decided by officials long gone, and critics of preclearance generally argue it treats states unequally based on past conduct rather than current proof.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For voters in covered jurisdictions the gains are substantial: advance review is designed to stop discriminatory voting changes before an election rather than after the damage is done, which ordinary litigation cannot do. The costs are real but administrative — added review, notice, and resource obligations for state and local governments, and a federal approval step for election administration. The bill includes a built-in exit: jurisdictions can win exemption through a declaratory judgment, and coverage lapses after 10 years without new violations.

outcome.mechanism: Leahy introduced the bill in June 2015 and the Senate Judiciary Committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, so it sat in committee until the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Sen. Patrick Leahy introduced the Voting Rights Advancement Act of 2015 on June 24, 2015, prompted by the need to revise the Voting Rights Act's coverage criteria for states and political subdivisions.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced; the complete action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.
Forty-five senators cosponsored the bill: 42 Democrats, 2 independents, and 1 Republican.
The bill would have replaced the Voting Rights Act coverage formula the Supreme Court invalidated, with states and localities covered for 10 years based on 25-year violation histories.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State and local election officials in jurisdictions that would have faced federal preclearance are better off, as are incumbent officeholders who benefit from the ability to change voting rules without advance federal review. Voters of color and tribal members, who would have gained advance protection, gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Jurisdictions avoiding federal review of voting changes

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor; it was referred to the Judiciary Committee, where he served as ranking member.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin and 23 other Democratic and independent senators
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors on the day of introduction.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it in committee without action.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote.

against.name: 53 of 54 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Did not cosponsor the bill; only one Republican joined.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic and independent — 42 of 44 Democrats plus both independents cosponsored, against 1 of 54 Republicans — and the Republican-controlled committee never acted.

industries.note: The bill would require advance federal approval or public notice for changes to voting rules, precinct resources, and district boundaries, and would obligate them to provide polling resources on tribal lands. Their interest in unrestricted control over election administration runs against the voters the bill would protect.

Preclearance and transparency requirements would constrain the ability to change election rules — ID requirements, district lines, polling locations — that incumbents can otherwise shape, with demographic data on district changes becoming public.
